extracted.intended_audience: journal editors and publishers implementing peer review; peer review researchers; journal reviewers
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, implementing, and evaluating a structured set of review questions for journal peer review (structured peer review), including recommended question wording, answer options, and metrics for assessing reviewer responses and inter-rater agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Q1. Are the objectives and the rationale of the study clearly stated?
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the objectives and the rationale of the study clearly stated?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of the structured questions piloted; intended to evaluate clarity of study objectives/rationale. Can be answered with Yes/No/N/A or with comments. Reported (partial) agreement in pilot was 58%.

rubrics_metrics.name: Q2. Reporting methods for replicability/reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: If applicable, is the application/theory/method/study reported in sufficient detail to allow for its replicability and/or reproducibility?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Piloted as an open-text question with Yes/No/N/A prompts inserted. Longest median answer length (Md 27 words). (Partial) agreement 60%. Recommendation: keep as a methods-focused question in structured review and provide free text for suggested changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Q3. Appropriateness and reporting of statistical analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: If applicable, are statistical analyses, controls, sampling mechanism, and statistical reporting (e.g., P-values, CIs, effect sizes) appropriate and well described?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Piloted with Yes/No/N/A prompts. (Partial) agreement was low (52%), highlighting common reviewer disagreement on core methodological aspects; reviewers should be asked to provide specific suggestions when answering 'No'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Q4. Need for additional/improved tables or figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Could the manuscript benefit from additional tables or figures, or from improving or removing (some of the) existing ones?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Piloted as open text. (Partial) agreement 64%. Note in initial pilot some questions had inverted answer meaning (Yes meant 'improvement needed'); authors recommend aligning answer direction across questions so Yes consistently means 'no change needed'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Q5. Are interpretations/conclusions supported by data?
rubrics_metrics.description: If applicable, are the interpretation of results and study conclusions supported by the data?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Piloted with Yes/No/N/A prompts. One of the lowest (partial) agreement items (53%)—flagged as an area of high disagreement and importance for editorial decision-making. Some reviewers skipped this question more often than others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Q6. Have authors emphasized study strengths?
rubrics_metrics.description: Have the authors clearly emphasized the strengths of their study/theory/methods/argument?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Piloted as open text. (Partial) agreement 64%. Rarely addressed in traditional reports (1% asked to emphasize strengths), indicating structured prompting can increase attention to strengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Q7. Have authors clearly stated limitations?
rubrics_metrics.description: Have the authors clearly stated the limitations of their study/methods?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Piloted as open text. (Partial) agreement 67%. This question was commonly handled by directing commenters to the Comments-to-Author field or attachments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Q8. Manuscript structure, flow, or writing need improvement?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the manuscript structure, flow or writing need improving (e.g., the addition of subheadings, shortening of text, reorganization of sections, or moving details from one section to another)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Piloted as open text. Highest (partial) agreement at 72%; reviewers converged more on structural/readability issues. Suggest presenting examples and concrete suggestions in free text when 'No' is selected (i.e., change needed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Q9. Could the manuscript benefit from language editing?
rubrics_metrics.description: Could the manuscript benefit from language editing?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Piloted as a yes/no drop-down (no free-text option). (Partial) agreement 58%. Recommendation: harmonize answer types so all questions use consistent answer formats (prefer multiple-choice with optional free-text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended set: Introduction Q1 – background/literature currency
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the background and literature section up to date and appropriate for the topic?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the authors' refined Box 1 recommendation (two questions per IMRaD section). Intended to prompt reviewer attention to literature currency and relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended set: Introduction Q2 – objectives clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the primary (and secondary) objectives clearly stated at the end of the introduction?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refined wording recommended to focus on explicit statement of objectives; supports editorial decisions and author self-checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended set: Methods Q3 – methods detail for replicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the study methods (including theory/applicability/modelling) reported in sufficient detail to allow for their replicability or reproducibility?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refinement of earlier methods question; recommendation to implement this as a multiple-choice question with a free-text option for suggested fixes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended set: Methods Q4 – statistical analyses and reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Are statistical analyses, controls, sampling mechanism, and statistical reporting (e.g., P-values, CIs, effect sizes) appropriate and well described?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refined recommended question for methods/statistics; authors recommend consistent answer options and optional free text for concrete suggestions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended set: Results Q5 – results presentation / tables & figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the results presentation, including the number of tables and figures, appropriate to best present the study findings?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refined question focusing on presentation and appropriateness of tables/figures; encourages reviewers to consider whether the visuals effectively communicate findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended set: Results Q6 – need for additional analyses/metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Are additional sub-analyses or statistical measures needed (e.g., reporting of CIs, effect sizes, sensitivity analyses)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompts reviewers to suggest concrete additional analyses; helpful for editors to know if substantive additional work is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended set: Discussion Q7 – interpretation supported by data/design
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the interpretation of results and study conclusions supported by the data and the study design?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refines Q5 to explicitly link interpretation to study design; recommended for consistent assessment of inferential claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended set: Discussion Q8 – limitations emphasized
rubrics_metrics.description: Have the authors clearly emphasized the limitations of their study/theory/methods/argument?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintains focus on transparent limitation reporting; recommended as one of eight core items reviewers should address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answer options / response format recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: We recommend questions of a multiple-choice style, with the last answer option having a free text field in which reviewers should provide constructive criticism to the authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended choices for all questions: [ ] Not Applicable; [ ] Beyond my expertise, additional reviewer(s) should be consulted; [ ] Yes; [ ] No, the authors should (consider): (please list and number in the text field below Your suggestions so that the author/s can more easily follow your instructions or provide rebuttals). Rationale: enables easier calculation of rater agreement and better readability for authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answer style coding scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: Coding categories applied to reviewer answers: 1) yes; 2) no; 3) not applicable; 4) yes, and provided comments to the authors on how to address the issue; 5) no, and provided comments to the authors on how to address the issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used for qualitative coding of responses; when calculating inter-rater agreement, responses were further categorized as Agreement (same category), Disagreement (different categories), Partial agreement (e.g., yes vs yes+comments), and Unable to assess (missing answer, N/A, or pointed to attachment). Authors combined Agreement and Partial agreement when reporting '(partial) agreement'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-rater agreement categories and reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Agreement categories for pairwise reviewer coding: A) agreement; B) disagreement; C) partial agreement; D) unable to assess agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For presentation, authors grouped A and C and reported (partial) agreement percentages per question and for final recommendations. Absolute agreement for final recommendations (exact match) was also tracked (41% in pilot).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer completion and uptake metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure reviewer uptake by percent answering structured questions, number of skipped questions, use of attachments, and direction to Comments-to-Author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pilot metrics: 92% of reviewers filled out all structured fields; small percentages skipped 1–2 questions; track which questions are skipped more often (question 5 was most skipped). Use these metrics to assess feasibility and adherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comments-to-Author usage and classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Track whether reviewers used the Comments-to-Author field, and classify content as: additional comments expanding on structured answers, or traditional full peer review reports copied into the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In pilot 68% filled Comments-to-Author; 72% of those were traditional full reports. Report median word counts (e.g., full reports Md 482 words). Also measure how many of the structured-question topics appear in traditional reports (median 4/9).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative evaluation metrics and statistical methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended metrics and analyses for evaluating structured peer review pilot outcomes: word counts (median, IQR), inter-rater (partial and absolute) agreement percentages, chi-square tests for agreement differences across fields/IF quartiles, Kruskal–Wallis for word count differences, odds ratios for associations (e.g., Comments-to-Author vs Comments-to-Editor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use non-parametric summarization where distributions are non-normal; report absolute and partial agreement, compare to historical baseline data where available; consider significance threshold P < 0.05.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unify answer direction and question phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure that answer direction is consistent across all questions (i.e., a 'Yes' should consistently indicate no change needed or vice versa).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pilot found that some questions (e.g., 4, 8, 9) were inverted relative to others, causing potential confusion; authors recommend modifying questions so answer direction and options are the same across all questions to reduce cognitive load and improve interpretability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementation practice recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational recommendations for implementing structured peer review in submission systems and in editorial workflows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notify reviewers in advance about the questions and encourage answering during manuscript reading; implement questions as multiple choice with optional free-text suggestions; allow editors to adapt question bank to field-specific needs; consider system support for measuring rater agreement and collecting attachments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of structured questions as author checklist / transparency tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommend that authors be informed of the structured questions in advance and can use them as a self-review checklist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors may use the same questions to prepare manuscripts; informing authors improves transparency on the criteria their work will be judged against and might improve manuscript quality pre-submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding and consensus process for qualitative answers
rubrics_metrics.description: Double independent coding of open-text answers with subsequent consensus meetings to agree on final codes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In pilot, two coders independently coded answers using an inductively developed codebook, then met to reconcile differences; initial independent absolute inter-rater agreement was 94%. Maintain reproducible codebook and store coding outputs for transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attachment and redirection handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for reviewers who direct readers to attachments or to Comments-to-Author instead of answering structured fields directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track frequency of redirection to attachments or Comments-to-Author; consider limiting or structuring attachments to ensure answers are accessible and assessable. In pilot, 7% directed to attachments and ~38% directed to Comments-to-Author for additional details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final recommendation tracking
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect and analyse reviewers' final recommendation choice (e.g., accept, revise, reject) and compute absolute agreement (exact match) between reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use absolute agreement as a performance metric for the structured approach; pilot showed a higher absolute agreement (41%) than historical Elsevier baseline (30%), but authors caution this was observational and not randomized.
